questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first question about a document
questions.learningObjective: Identify the first question to ask of a document
questions.stem: An engineer drafting a canal-brief finds a 1763 ledger and wants its opening question settled before quoting it.

options.text: Ask who made the document and for what purpose before drawing on its contents
Ask what the document says about the year of construction before anything else
options.misconception: reads content before provenance

options.text: Ask whether the entries are legible enough to be used in the final brief
options.misconception: assumes legibility settles the question

options.text: Ask whether other engineers have already quoted the same ledger
options.misconception: treats later citation as origin

questions.explanation: The first question about a document concerns its making: who wrote it and for whom. Reading the contents first treats the ledger as a plain window on the past, and misses the purpose that shaped it.
questions.hint: Ask about the maker before the message.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Decide when a second account counts as independent
questions.stem: Consulting a 1789 warehouse inventory, an engineer seeks a second account of the same roof collapse that does not simply echo the first.

options.text: Treat the second account as independent only if a different scribe wrote it
options.misconception: assumes a new hand breaks shared dependence

options.text: Treat the second account as independent only if it rests on a separate chain of witnesses
Treat the second account as independent because it appeared in a later printed book
options.misconception: confuses later printing with separate origin

options.text: Treat the second account as independent as soon as it adds detail the first lacks
options.misconception: reads extra detail as a free-standing source

questions.explanation: Independence means the second account did not draw on the first. A different hand, a later print or added detail can reproduce the same chain of witnesses, so agreement between them proves little.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second account copied the first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: State what a customs register can and cannot establish
questions.stem: A customs register for 1805 lists 42 barrels of pitch in one entry and 47 in a later page, and an engineer is asked what the book can prove.

options.text: It establishes that exactly 47 barrels passed through the port that year
options.misconception: treats a ledger total as a complete census

options.text: It establishes that every barrel on the quay was taxed at the same rate
options.misconception: assumes uniform rating across all cargo

options.text: It establishes what the customs house itself recorded in those entries
It establishes that pitch exports rose sharply across the following decade
options.misconception: reads one year as a trend

questions.explanation: A customs register fixes what the office recorded, not what actually passed the quay. The mismatch between 42 and 47 shows clerical variance, not a physical shortfall in the trade.
questions.hint: Ask what the clerks wrote, not what the harbour held.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how genre limits a document's evidentiary use
questions.stem: Reusing a 1790 mill document in a heritage brief, an engineer must explain how the document's genre shapes what it can be used to prove.

answer.exemplar: A genre is the social form a document takes because someone needed it for that purpose. A pamphlet written to persuade shapes its claims around the need to persuade and around who was listening, so the engineer must ask what the form was for before deciding what it proves. The persuasive pressure also tells him where to look for strain, since a writer aiming at an audience is likely to present the case in its tidiest light.

questions.explanation: Genre fixes the purpose a document was made for, and that purpose limits what it records. A petition made to press a case cannot be read as a neutral tally of what happened.
questions.hint: Ask what the form was made to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Judging the past by its own moment
questions.learningObjective: Judge a source by the standards of its own moment

stimulus.body: By order of the burgess council, no cart or wagon shall pass over the new stone bridge between the third hour before dawn and the fifth hour after sunrise, so that the carriers of grain may cross in daylight. The order is signed by two of the aldermen and dated the eleventh day of March.

questions.stem: Drafting a pedestrian bridge brief, an engineer reads a 1761 municipal order about cart traffic and asks what it licenses him to claim.

options.text: That carts were a recognised traffic at that hour and the stone bridge already stood
That the bridge opened only to pedestrians for its first three hours each day
options.misconception: misreads a timing rule as a closure

options.text: That stone spans of that period carried no loads above half a ton
options.misconception: treats a rule about hours as a load limit

options.text: That the council intended to abolish heavy freight from the town entirely
options.misconception: reads a limited restriction as total policy

questions.explanation: Reading the order on its own terms shows it regulated cart hours in 1761, not the bridge's strength. It shows carts used the stone span and that the masonry was in place; it is silent on tonnage.
questions.hint: Read the order as a traffic rule of its day.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Combine what an account book shows with what it omits
questions.stem: Preparing a weighhouse restoration brief, an engineer must work out what a 1788 account book establishes and what it leaves open.

options.text: It establishes total trade passing through the weighhouse for the year 1788
options.misconception: reads a single yardbook as a complete trade record

options.text: It establishes the entries the clerk chose to record and the sums still owed
It establishes the true profit the weighhouse made across its working life
options.misconception: assumes one book spans the business lifetime

options.text: It establishes which merchants were honest in settling their accounts
options.misconception: turns a debt column into a moral judgement

questions.explanation: An account book records the clerk's chosen entries, so it fixes what was written and owed.
questions.hint: Say what was written and what was still owed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the argument a map is making
questions.stem: A county surveyor in 1812 drew a proposed new road on a map that made the old crossing look narrow and steep.

options.text: It records the exact gradients the survey party measured on the ground
options.misconception: reads a drawing as a field measurement

options.text: It proves the old road could never have carried a loaded wagon
options.misconception: treats a rhetorical map as a load certificate

options.text: It argues for the new route by presenting the old one unfavourably
It fixes the legal boundary of the parish at the date of survey
options.misconception: confuses a route proposal with a boundary record

questions.explanation: A map made to support a proposal is an argument in drawing: it selects features and omits others to make the case. Reading it as measured ground data mistakes persuasion for survey.
questions.hint: Ask what the map was made to persuade.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a list of names as a record of patronage
questions.stem: Renovating a civic hall, an engineer reads a 1720 plaque naming the mayor who paid for the rebuild and the guilds who supplied timber.

options.text: That the hall was rebuilt entirely at the mayor's own expense
options.misconception: reads one named donor as sole sponsor

options.text: That the timber guilds held the deciding vote on the project
options.misconception: confuses supply with authority

options.text: That no other funding source existed besides those named
options.misconception: treats a selective list as complete

options.text: That the named parties were the ones the plaque wished seen as patrons

questions.explanation: A dedication plaque names who deserved public credit, so it tells us about the choice of names rather than the whole funding picture. Its silences are as deliberate as its entries.
questions.hint: Ask who wanted to be named, and why.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Show that translation involves interpretive choice
questions.stem: A 1740 Portuguese survey reaches an engineer in two English versions whose wordings differ in 14 places, and he must cite one in the brief.

options.text: That translation involves choice, so the choice must be defended in the brief
That the later English version is the more accurate of the two renderings
options.misconception: assumes later means more accurate

options.text: That the original Portuguese text must contain errors wherever the versions differ
options.misconception: reads difference as error in the source

options.text: That the engineer should quote both versions to avoid making any choice at all
options.misconception: believes refusing to choose avoids the problem

questions.explanation: Where renderings differ, each choice argues for one reading of the original, so a citation must be defended. Counting the 14 differences shows translation is interpretive.
questions.hint: Differences show interpretation, not correctness.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the date of an act from the date of its record
questions.stem: A deeds bundle dated 1785 turns out to have been recopied in 1811 by a clerk who tidied the margins.

answer.exemplar: The bundle proves two different things on two different dates. The 1785 deed records the transaction as it was understood then; the 1811 copy is evidence of how that clerk found it, including what was tidied or omitted. The engineer should cite the 1785 act for its terms and the 1811 copy only for what the later clerk preserved, corrected or left out.

questions.explanation: Two dates matter: when the deed was made and when the surviving text was written. A tidy 1811 copy may carry 1785 content faithfully, but its phrasing is the clerk's.
questions.hint: Each layer belongs to its own date.

questions.topic: The first question about a document
questions.learningObjective: Identify the opening question that frames a document

stimulus.body: Memorandum of the casting house of Fenwick and Sons, entered on the day of the order. The writer sets down first the business for which the record is kept, and only afterwards the particulars of the customer and the goods required.

questions.stem: Choosing cast iron for a pump house, an engineer finds a foundry memo that opens by stating the business for which it was written.

options.text: How many of each casting the customer had ordered
options.misconception: starts with quantity rather than purpose

options.text: Who the customer was and what the castings were for
options.misconception: asks only for the customer name

options.text: Why the casting house was writing the order down at all
What the castings had cost the customer in the past year
options.misconception: assumes the memo is an invoice

questions.explanation: A memo states its purpose first, and that purpose frames everything after it. Whether the details are a count, a customer record or a price depends on why the casting house wrote the memo down.
questions.hint: Read the opening for the reason for writing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Combine two records without letting either override the other
questions.stem: Two engineers brief a shared footbridge: one cites a parish minute book of 1809, the other a surveyor's report of 1811.

options.text: Treat the minute book as decisive because it was kept by an official body
options.misconception: ranks documents by official status alone

options.text: Treat the survey report as decisive because it was produced later
options.misconception: assumes later documents are truer

options.text: Treat the two as showing what each office needed to record
options.misconception: reads each file without comparing purposes

options.text: Treat each as evidence of what its own authors needed to establish

questions.explanation: The two records answer different questions because different offices made them, so neither automatically wins. Setting eachst its purpose shows where they can be joined and where they must stay apart.
questions.hint: Compare what each office needed to know.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the limits of a surviving customs volume
questions.stem: A canal company's 1830 customs register survives in a bound volume with gaps where a clerk had torn out pages.

options.text: The entries the clerk chose to write down, and the gaps where pages were removed
The complete tonnage of goods carried along the canal in 1830
options.misconception: treats a surviving volume as a complete series

options.text: That the missing pages held the most valuable cargo entries
options.misconception: invents content for missing pages

options.text: The names of every shipping company that used the canal
options.misconception: assumes the register lists firms rather than goods

questions.explanation: A register with removed pages is evidence of what was recorded and of a break in the record itself. The missing pages tell the engineer that the volume is now a partial witness.
questions.hint: Say what survives and what is lost.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a document's genre from what it does
questions.stem: Drafting a heritage statement, an engineer must classify a 1798 sheet as a gazette, a lease, a sermon, or a custom roll.

options.text: Gazette, because it announces matters officially to a wide readership
options.misconception: confuses official tone with official form

options.text: Custom roll, because it records duties due on listed goods
Lease, because it fixes obligations between two named parties
options.misconception: sees binding obligations in every list

options.text: Sermon, because it opens with a paragraph of moral instruction
options.misconception: takes elevated tone as moral teaching

questions.explanation: Genre is identified by the job the document does. A custom roll's job is to list goods and the duties owed on them, which is what the sheet does; tone and address do not decide the form.
questions.hint: Identify the job the sheet was made to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Judging the past by its own moment
questions.learningObjective: Compare a stated rule with practice in the same period
questions.stem: A 1650 guild ordinance bans carts on a bridge at night, while a 1712 repair account records 40 night deliveries to the mill.

options.text: That the 1650 ban was ignored without consequence from the start
options.misconception: reads later breach as proof of early defiance

options.text: That the 1712 deliveries were made before the ban was issued
options.misconception: reverses the order of the documents

options.text: That the rule existed while the practice it forbade continued
That the 1712 deliveries prove the ban had been formally repealed
options.misconception: treats practice as legal repeal

questions.explanation: A rule on paper and a practice on the ground can coexist for decades. The ordinance shows the council's stated intent; the account of 40 deliveries shows what the mill actually did.
questions.hint: A rule and a practice can both be true.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how internal checks test an account book's reliability
questions.stem: An engineer writing a brief on a granary must explain how the 1783 account book's double-entry columns let him test its own reliability.

answer.exemplar: Because every sum appears in both a debit and a credit column, the book can be checked against itself. Where the two sides do not balance, the engineer knows a line was mistyped or deliberately adjusted, and can either reject the entry or ask who gained. Where they balance, the totals are internally consistent, though still silent on anything the clerk chose not to record at all.

questions.explanation: Double entry records each sum twice, so a mismatch between the debit and credit columns flags an error. That internal check makes the book more testable than a single column of totals.
questions.hint: Check the two columns against each other.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a map produced to justify a route

stimulus.body: Survey of the proposed line, drawn to accompany the directors' printed notice. The existing turnpike road is shown contracted to a narrow hairpin between the mill and the ford; the proposed straight line is drawn wide and level.

questions.stem: A railway company's 1830 survey map shows the existing road as a hairpin and the new line as a gentle sweep, and an engineer must justify the chosen route.

options.text: The map is neutral because it was produced by a professional survey office
options.misconception: assumes expertise removes persuasion

options.text: The map argues for the new line by shaping how the old one appears
The map proves the old road was too steep for any loaded cart
options.misconception: reads a drawn exaggeration as survey data

options.text: The map is inadmissible because a company paid for it
options.misconception: dismisses a paid source as worthless

questions.explanation: A map drawn to justify a scheme carries its maker's interests in the choices it makes. The engineer may use it, but should name the company's stake and treat the contrast as argument, not measurement.
questions.hint: Ask who commissioned the map and why.

questions.learningObjective: Combine ranks and property marks in a guild listing
questions.stem: A guild charter lists the master, two wardens and nine journeymen, but names only one of the two wardens as a property holder.

options.text: That guild membership was open to anyone in the town without property
options.misconception: ignores the property qualifier

options.text: That the guild elected its own leaders in open session each year
options.misconception: infers a procedure from a list of names

options.text: That rank inside the guild tracked wealth as well as length of service
That the missing warden's name has been deliberately suppressed
options.misconception: infers suppression from a simple omission

questions.explanation: The list shows who held office and what the compiler recorded about their wealth. Only one warden appears as a property holder, suggesting rank tracked wealth as well as service.
questions.hint: Read ranks and property marks together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define translation as a reading rather than a copy
questions.stem: A translation of a 1689 order survives only in an 1810 English version prepared for an insurance company.

options.text: A faithful copy of words with no change of sense
options.misconception: believes translation is word-for-word copying

options.text: A record of what the original said before any later copying
options.misconception: confuses the original with the copy

options.text: The final stage in a document's life before it is archived
options.misconception: treats translation as archival finishing

options.text: A reading of the original that must be argued for and can be disputed

questions.explanation: Translation is a reading, not a copy, so every version rests on choices about sense, register and legal weight. The 1810 English version was made for an insurer, which shapes the choices it made.
questions.hint: A translation argues for one reading of a text.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Date a source by its moment of composition
questions.stem: Choosing archival glass for a reading room, an engineer consults a 1764 gazette printed to correct a rumour spread the year before.

options.text: The date of printing, because the gazette answers a claim made in 1763
The date of the rumour, because the gazette was written to counter it
options.misconception: takes the subject's date as the source's date

options.text: The date of the paper contract that paid for the printing
options.misconception: confuses production arrangements with composition

options.text: The date of the earliest surviving copy of the gazette
options.misconception: uses transmission date as date of writing

questions.explanation: A source is dated by when it was written, not by the event it discusses or by a later copy's travel. Since this gazette answers a 1763 rumour, its position and tone follow from its 1764 purpose.
questions.hint: Date the writing, not the subject.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first question about a document
questions.learningObjective: Measure what a set of documents records about its own practice
questions.stem: Three slips in a 1702 binding shop ledger begin with the same phrase, and an engineer counts how many of them name the customer.

options.text: Only slips that record the customer can establish what the shop supplied
options.misconception: makes one field decide the whole document

options.text: The count of customer-named slips shows how consistently the shop recorded clients
The three slips together prove the shop served one family for years
options.misconception: reads a repeated phrase as one continuous patron

options.text: The slips show that the shop's records survive only for its richest clients
options.misconception: infers wealth bias from a small sample

questions.explanation: Counting how many of the three slips name a customer measures the shop's recording habit, nothing more. It cannot show how long any family was served.
questions.hint: A count measures the recorder, not the trade.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why differing dates do not guarantee independence
questions.stem: Because two accounts of the 1832 flood were written apart, an engineer must explain why they are still not independent.

answer.exemplar: Independence is a question of transmission, not of handwriting. If both accounts draw on the same earlier newspaper report or the same set of eye-witnesses, then agreement between them adds no confirmation of the event itself. The engineer should trace where each account got its information, note any shared source, and describe the points where the accounts diverge as the only places where genuine corroboration is possible.

questions.explanation: Different hands and dates do not make accounts independent; each may draw on the same report or witnesses. Independence must be traced along the chain of transmission, not assumed from the date.
questions.hint: Trace the chain of transmission, not the dates.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: Keep unlike units separate when comparing entries
questions.stem: A customs register lists salt by the bushel and silk by the piece, and an engineer must build a brief that compares the trade honestly.

options.text: By keeping each commodity in its own recorded unit rather than forcing one total
By converting every entry to the bushel so one single total can be shown
options.misconception: assumes units can be silently equated

options.text: By ignoring the silk, which is too small to affect the overall trade
options.misconception: drops small items from the record

options.text: By reporting only the salt, since only it appears in every surviving year
options.misconception: selects on survival instead of substance

questions.explanation: Goods counted in different units cannot be added without a conversion the register never makes. Reporting each commodity in its own unit keeps the evidence intact.
questions.hint: Do not total what was never totalled.

questions.learningObjective: Classify a document by the job its columns perform
questions.stem: An engineer's clerk classifies a 1720 sheet of parish poor rates and finds it lists names, sums and dates in a ruled table.

options.text: A private letter, because the entries are in a personal hand
options.misconception: judges genre by handwriting alone

options.text: A chronicle, because the entries run in date order over years

options.text: A rate roll, because it lists assessments due and their dates

questions.topic: Judging the past by its own moment
questions.learningObjective: Judge a historical remark by its own standards
questions.stem: A 1602 town record describes a bridge as adequate for carriages that today would be judged unsafe.

options.text: Judge the bridge by the traffic and loading standards of 1602
Apply present safety standards, since the masonry itself has not changed
options.misconception: assumes modern standards apply to old work

options.text: Reject the record, since no engineer of that era knew how to build a bridge

options.text: Accept the bridge as safe because townsmen had used it for many years
options.misconception: treats long use as proof of safety

questions.learningObjective: Report a discrepancy in an account book rather than smoothing it
questions.stem: A 1770 account book shows 12 loads of coal received and 9 loads of coal paid for, and an engineer's brief needs the discrepancy handled.

options.text: The engineer should treat the 12 loads as the true quantity handled
options.misconception: picks the larger figure without a reason

options.text: The engineer should note the 3-load gap as an open point in the record
The engineer should average the two figures to get ten and a half loads
options.misconception: averages two incompatible counts

options.text: The engineer should treat the 9 loads as coal already sold onward
options.misconception: assumes the smaller figure records onward sales

questions.explanation: Twelve received against nine paid for leaves three loads unaccounted for, and the brief should say so. Choosing one figure or averaging them invents a total the book does not contain.
questions.hint: Report the gap rather than smoothing it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a proposal map differs from a survey
questions.stem: Explaining in a brief how a 1795 county map was drawn to argue for a new turnpike rather than to survey the ground, an engineer shows why.

answer.exemplar: The county map was made inside a turnpike campaign, and that tells the engineer how to read its choices. The old road is drawn narrow and steep where the new line is drawn broad and level, which is a comparison the survey itself did not require. The map is therefore good evidence that the county argued for a new road, and weak evidence about gradients, widths or the actual cost of either route. Read with the minutes and the subscription list, its purpose becomes visible.

questions.explanation: A map can persuade, enlarging some features and omitting others. Where a route proposal is drawn, the contrast between old and new roads is part of the case.
questions.hint: Read the picture alongside the minutes.

questions.learningObjective: Judge what a tax list of names can be used to claim

stimulus.body: Land tax list for the parish of Nettlebed, 1750. Each entry gives the name of the householder, the surname of his wife where she was taxed in the same household, and the amount assessed on the land.

options.text: That the wives listed held property in their own right

options.text: That the list was compiled for a cadastral survey of the county
options.misconception: confuses tax purpose with survey purpose

options.text: That the compiler recorded who was seen as heading a household

questions.explanation: A tax list names taxable householders as the law and compiler saw them, including wives recorded in a man's household. It shows how the parish presented its people, not a census or women's holdings.
questions.hint: Ask what the compiler was obliged to record.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Test an unusual entry date against the document's own practice
questions.stem: A foundry's day book for 1840 has entries for a Tuesday and, in a second hand, a Sunday, and an engineer must date the castings.

answer.exemplar: The names on the list are the compiler's choices, and choices carry a point of view. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a customs register can establish
questions.learningObjective: Explain why silence in a register proves very little
questions.stem: An unrecorded commodity prompts an engineer to explain why a customs register's silence about it proves so little.

answer.exemplar: Silence in a customs register is a fact about the register, not about the trade. Entries were made for goods that were assessed, and some goods escaped assessment entirely through exemption, fraud or simple neglect, while whole pages are often lost. The engineer should therefore treat an unrecorded commodity as unknown rather than absent, look for other registers or private accounts that cover the same period, and describe the gap in the brief rather than allowing the reader to infer a halt in traffic.

questions.explanation: Registers recorded duties on taxed goods and omitted what escaped assessment. A commodity's absence may reflect tax policy, exemption, smuggling or a lost page, so absence is not proof it never moved.
questions.hint: Absence of record is not absence of trade.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Cite a charter and its later reprint as two sources
questions.stem: Citing a 1768 charter and its 1890 reprint requires an engineer to explain why they are two sources, not one.

answer.exemplar: A reprint is a new act of transmission, and it should be cited as one. The 1890 printer chose what to reproduce, corrected what he thought was wrong and passed over what did not suit him, none of which the 1768 charter can have done to itself. The engineer should cite the charter for what was enacted in 1768, cite the reprint separately for what was known and believed in 1890, and record the differences between them as evidence of changing understanding rather than of the original text's uncertainty.

questions.explanation: The charter dates from 1768 and the reprint from 1890, so the printed text carries an editor's corrections and silences. Citing them as one source collapses that hand's work into the original act.
questions.hint: An act and a reading of it are different things.
